paragraphs: Data-driven methods for partial differential equations can make solving these equations faster, but training them requires many accurate examples. Producing those examples can itself be computationally expensive. DiffOAS addresses this preparation cost by changing how training data are generated, with the stated aim of improving both generation speed and numerical precision.

The method starts with a small collection of basic PDE solutions and combines them to obtain additional solutions. It then applies differential operators to those solutions to produce PDE data points. This places the reusable solutions at the center of data generation, allowing the algorithm to build a larger dataset through combinations and operator evaluations.

The theoretical analysis finds a time complexity one order lower than the existing generation method. In the reported experiments, generating 10,000 instances is 300 times faster. A neural operator trained on DiffOAS data also achieves comparable performance using only 5% of the generation time. These results connect faster data preparation to the practical objective: training a useful PDE model.
icml-2024-accelerating-pde-data-generati.tldr: DiffOAS combines basic PDE solutions and applies differential operators to generate accurate training data much faster in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: AnyTool tackles the problem of answering user requests using a very large collection of APIs. Its setting includes more than 16,000 APIs from Rapid API, under the assumption that some subset could potentially solve the request. The challenge is to find useful candidates, use them effectively, and recover when an attempted solution is impracticable.

The system divides this work among three components. A hierarchical retriever identifies candidate APIs, a solver attempts the task with the selected candidates, and a self-reflection mechanism reactivates the system when the initial solution cannot work. AnyTool uses GPT-4 function calling, so its design does not require training separate external modules.

The paper also identifies an evaluation weakness that can inflate pass rates and introduces a revised protocol alongside AnyToolBench. Across the evaluated datasets, AnyTool outperforms ToolLLM and a GPT-4 variant adapted for tool use. The abstract reports a +35.5% average pass-rate advantage over ToolLLM on ToolBench. The contribution therefore covers both agent design and how practical success is measured.
icml-2024-anytool-self-reflective-hierar.tldr: AnyTool combines hierarchical API retrieval, task solving, and self-reflection to improve tool use across a collection of more than 16,000 APIs.

paragraphs: When labels are noisy, collecting several judgments for each example and taking a majority vote seems like a natural way to improve an evaluation. This paper asks whether that is the best use of a fixed labeling budget when the specific goal is to determine which of two binary classifiers is more accurate.

The authors prove that, in the comparison problem they study, the budget is better spent obtaining one label for each of more examples. The distinction is between improving an individual example’s label and improving the overall decision about which classifier wins. Spending labels repeatedly on the same example can sacrifice the broader coverage that helps make that comparison.

The proof uses Cramér’s theorem from large-deviation theory to analyze the comparison. It also yields sample-size bounds that improve on those obtained from Hoeffding’s bound. These findings challenge familiar recommendations for benchmark construction: when the objective is ranking two binary classifiers, the most useful labeling strategy need not be the one that produces the cleanest labels for individual examples.
icml-2024-dont-label-twice-quantity-beat.tldr: For the studied task of comparing two binary classifiers, labeling more examples once is better than spending the same budget on repeated labels.

paragraphs: Distributed learning must sometimes tolerate workers that send faulty or adversarial updates. Many robust methods assume that the same workers remain faulty throughout training. This paper addresses a more dynamic situation, where malfunctions are intermittent or attacks affect different workers at different times, changing which updates can be trusted.

The proposed method, DynaBRO, supports any sublinear number of changes in faulty-worker identities across training rounds. Sublinear means that the number of changes grows more slowly than the total number of rounds. At the server, DynaBRO applies multi-level Monte Carlo gradient estimation to worker updates that have already been robustly aggregated. An adaptive learning rate removes the need to know the fraction of faulty workers beforehand.

When identity changes number O(√T), with T denoting training rounds, the method nearly matches the best stated asymptotic convergence rate for the static setting. The result shows that allowing worker identities to change need not destroy strong convergence behavior when those changes satisfy the specified growth condition.
icml-2024-dynamic-byzantine-robust-learn.tldr: DynaBRO tolerates changing faulty workers and nearly matches static-setting convergence rates when identity changes grow as O(√T).

paragraphs: A language model’s key-value cache stores information from earlier tokens so decoding can reuse previous computation. That shortcut creates a memory bottleneck as more information accumulates. Existing compression methods reduce memory by dropping many cached entries, but this can hurt tasks that require recalling information spread across much of the earlier text.

LESS supplements eviction-based methods with a constant-sized cache described as nearly free. The additional cache retains information over time so that all tokens can still be queried at later decoding steps. Its purpose is to preserve a route to earlier information while continuing to benefit from the memory savings of removing individual cache entries.

Across a variety of tasks, the reported results show that LESS narrows the performance gap between compressed caching and retaining the full cache. In some cases it matches full-cache performance while remaining efficient. The finding supports this combination of selective retention and a compact persistent memory, particularly for tasks where discarding earlier information would otherwise reduce performance.
icml-2024-get-more-with-less-synthesizin.tldr: LESS adds a constant-sized memory to cache-eviction methods, helping preserve earlier-token information and sometimes matching full-cache performance.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding uses a smaller draft model to propose text that a larger language model then verifies. This can reduce generation latency, but the draft model’s design and the choice of proposals affect how much speed is gained. This paper introduces two modifications intended to improve decoding speed while keeping the target language model frozen.

GliDe changes the draft model so it can reuse the target model’s cached keys and values. CaPE changes proposal expansion: it uses the draft model’s confidence scores to select additional candidate tokens for verification. The two contributions act on different parts of the process, improving how the draft is produced and how the set of candidates is assembled.

Experiments across different benchmarks show that GliDe substantially reduces expected decoding latency. Measurements of actual elapsed time report speedups of up to 2.17 times for Vicuna models, increasing to 2.61 times with CaPE. These are reported maxima from the evaluations. Together, the results show that modifying the drafting and proposal stages can accelerate a fixed target model.
icml-2024-glide-with-a-cape-a-low-hassle.tldr: GliDe reuses target-model caches and CaPE expands proposals using confidence, achieving reported Vicuna decoding speedups of up to 2.61 times together.

paragraphs: Two learning agents can repeatedly interact while learning separately and pursuing objectives that do not fully agree. The paper models such interactions as Stackelberg games and asks how each player’s utility develops during learning. A central concern is regret: the accumulated shortfall relative to a chosen performance benchmark.

The authors show that standard benchmarks, including Stackelberg equilibrium payoffs, produce worst-case regret that grows linearly for at least one player. They therefore construct a relaxed benchmark that tolerates small learning errors. This changes what counts as a reasonable comparison when each agent is still adapting, but standard learning algorithms still fail to achieve sublinear regret under the new benchmarks.

The proposed algorithms achieve near-optimal O(T^(2/3)) regret for both players over T rounds. Because this grows more slowly than T, average regret decreases as interaction continues. In additionally relaxed environments, the authors obtain the faster O(√T) rate. These results connect the choice of benchmark and environment to what both independently learning players can achieve.
icml-2024-impact-of-decentralized-learni.tldr: Error-tolerant benchmarks and new algorithms enable near-optimal sublinear regret for both players in decentralized Stackelberg learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether language models can improve their answers through discussion among multiple model instances. Each instance first proposes its own response and reasoning. The instances then debate over several rounds, working toward a shared final answer. This adds an interaction process around existing models as another way to improve their responses.

The approach complements prompting methods such as checking an answer, considering multiple responses, or writing intermediate reasoning. Here, the proposed answers and explanations become material for further exchanges among the instances. The method can be applied directly to black-box models, and the authors use the same procedure and prompts across all tasks they investigate.

The reported findings show significant improvements in mathematical and strategic reasoning across several tasks. The authors also find improved factual validity, with fewer fallacious answers and hallucinations. These results support debate as a useful way to organize model inference in the evaluated settings. The broader suggestion is that structured interaction among instances may unlock capabilities beyond those obtained from an individual response.
icml-2024-improving-factuality-and-reaso.tldr: Multiple language-model instances debating their answers improve reasoning and factual accuracy across the tasks studied.

paragraphs: Representing language-model numbers with four bits can help meet latency and power requirements, but the numerical format affects accuracy and hardware cost. The authors analyze weights and activations across 30 networks and find that most of their distributions follow Student’s t-distribution. They use that observation to guide the design of low-precision formats.

The resulting Student Float format, SF4, is derived as theoretically optimal under the distributional model. It improves on NF4 across modern language models, including a reported 0.76% increase in average task accuracy for LLaMA2-7B. The authors then use SF4 as a high-accuracy reference when designing two variants of E2M1 with supernormal support.

An evaluation of 11 datatypes compares model accuracy with hardware complexity. INT4, E2M1, and E2M1 with supernormal support form the reported Pareto curve, describing different accuracy–chip-area tradeoffs. One example improves Phi-2 accuracy by up to 2.19% with 1.22% area overhead. The findings show why numerical-format choices should be assessed jointly for model quality and implementation cost.
icml-2024-learning-from-students-applyin.tldr: An analysis of LLM number distributions motivates four-bit formats with improved accuracy and measured tradeoffs in chip area.

paragraphs: IRED treats reasoning and decision-making as optimization problems. It learns energy functions that represent constraints linking an input to a desired output. Producing an answer then involves optimizing against those learned constraints, giving the model an iterative procedure that can continue for different numbers of steps depending on the difficulty of the problem.

Two techniques support this design. First, the method learns a sequence of annealed energy landscapes to make inference easier. Second, training combines supervision of the score function with supervision of the energy landscape, which the authors describe as making training faster and more stable. These techniques address both learning the constraints and using them effectively afterward.

The reported experiments show stronger performance than existing methods on continuous reasoning, discrete reasoning, and planning, especially in harder cases. IRED also solves examples beyond its training distribution, including more complex Sudoku puzzles, matrix completion with larger values, and path finding in larger graphs. These findings support adapting inference effort to difficulty as a way to extend the usefulness of learned reasoning constraints.
icml-2024-learning-iterative-reasoning-t.tldr: IRED learns energy-based constraints and adapts its optimization effort to solve harder reasoning and planning problems beyond its training distribution.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows use constrained transformations to represent probability distributions. Those architectural restrictions make their expressive power an important theoretical question: which distributions can a given family represent? The paper addresses a weakness in earlier universality results, which depended on allowing neural networks to become arbitrarily ill-conditioned, reducing their practical relevance.

The authors establish a distributional universality theorem for well-conditioned coupling-based flows, including architectures such as RealNVP. The significance is that broad expressive power can be established without relying on increasingly poor conditioning. This strengthens the theoretical justification for a widely used family of flow architectures.

The paper also shows that volume-preserving flows are not universal. It characterizes the distribution they learn instead and explains how their expressivity can be repaired. Together, these results distinguish two architectural families that might otherwise appear similarly capable. They support the general view that affine and related couplings are expressive and often outperform volume-preserving alternatives, helping connect observed performance differences with the structural constraints imposed by each design.
icml-2024-on-the-universality-of-volume-.tldr: The paper proves universality for well-conditioned coupling flows and characterizes the expressive limits of volume-preserving flows and how to repair them.

paragraphs: Guardrails filter inputs to language models or outputs from them to help mitigate risks. This position paper argues that building effective guardrails requires systematic design that takes the application context seriously. It examines open-source approaches, including Llama Guard, Nvidia NeMo, and Guardrails AI, to discuss challenges and paths toward more complete solutions.

The proposed process begins with socio-technical work involving a multidisciplinary team. The aim is to translate the needs and risks of an application into precise technical requirements. This matters because guardrail behavior depends on what a system is being used for and how its outputs affect people, so requirements must account for diverse contexts.

The authors then advocate exploring neural-symbolic implementations to handle complex requirements and developing verification and testing to assess the resulting product. The paper’s contribution is a design position grounded in previous research. It brings requirements, implementation, and assurance into one process, arguing that all three deserve attention when building safeguards for language-model applications.
icml-2024-position-building-guardrails-f.tldr: This position paper advocates context-sensitive guardrail design combining multidisciplinary requirements work, neural-symbolic implementation, and verification.

paragraphs: This position paper argues for building large generative systems by combining smaller generative models. Its starting point is the dominance of large, monolithic models trained on massive datasets. The proposed alternative makes composition a central design principle, so a system’s capabilities can emerge from how its constituent models are assembled.

The authors show how this approach can learn distributions more efficiently from data and generalize to regions of a distribution that were absent during training. The important connection is between reusable components and generalization: combining learned parts can provide a way to represent more than the particular data configurations encountered during learning.

The paper further shows how composition can support programming new generative models for tasks that were entirely unseen during training. It also reports that separate components can, in many cases, be discovered from data. These claims give composition two roles: a method for constructing new capabilities and a possible organizing structure for learning itself. The position encourages treating model assembly as a substantive part of generative-model design.
icml-2024-position-compositional-generat.tldr: The paper argues that composing smaller generative models can improve data efficiency and enable generalization to unseen data regions and tasks.

paragraphs: A regression model can predict accurately on ordinary inputs yet respond poorly when an adversary perturbs them at test time. This paper studies that tension in linear regression. It asks how much adversarial robustness is attainable while keeping standard predictive performance at a specified level, making the relationship between the two objectives quantitative.

The analysis distinguishes settings in which robustness can be obtained without sacrificing ordinary accuracy from settings in which a tradeoff might be unavoidable. That distinction matters because it avoids treating robustness as carrying the same accuracy cost in every problem. The conclusions instead depend on which regime the regression problem occupies.

The framework accommodates arbitrary feature covariance matrices and attack norms. These describe, respectively, relationships among input features and how allowed perturbations are measured. This broadens the coverage of earlier work. Simple experiments spanning several settings confirm the theoretical findings empirically. The contribution is therefore a more precise account of attainable robustness, including when preserving standard accuracy is compatible with it.
icml-2024-precise-accuracy-robustness-tr.tldr: The paper characterizes achievable robustness in linear regression and separates regimes with no accuracy cost from those where a tradeoff may be unavoidable.

paragraphs: Generating text under soft constraints can be formulated as sampling from an energy-based model. The difficulty is that text consists of discrete choices, while a language model’s internal energy calculations are differentiable. Gradients could guide sampling, but using them must still preserve the probability distribution the procedure is supposed to sample from.

The authors identify incorrect target sampling as a problem with previous attempts to extend gradient-based Markov chain Monte Carlo to text. They propose a solution and several variants, then study their theoretical properties. The central contribution is a principled way to use gradient information for discrete text sampling while retaining the target distribution.

Experiments covering several forms of text generation show that the proposed unbiased samplers produce more fluent text and better satisfy the control objectives. These findings link the theoretical sampling correction to practical generation quality. The authors also note that the methods could apply to discrete energy-based models outside language, making text an application of a potentially broader sampling approach.
icml-2024-principled-gradient-based-mcmc.tldr: The paper develops unbiased gradient-based samplers for discrete text, improving fluency and adherence to soft constraints in its experiments.

paragraphs: Releasing useful versions of sensitive tabular datasets requires a way to preserve information while protecting the underlying records. This paper studies differentially private data synthesis, with healthcare and government as motivating domains. Its focus is the generation of synthetic data from private estimates of marginal distributions, which summarize selected aspects of the original data.

PrivPGD introduces a new generation method within this marginal-based approach. It uses tools from optimal transport and particle gradient descent to construct the synthetic dataset. The contribution therefore concerns how private statistical estimates are turned into data that can be released, a central step in making those estimates useful.

The authors report that PrivPGD outperforms existing methods across a large range of datasets while remaining highly scalable. They also emphasize its ability to incorporate additional constraints specific to an application domain. These findings matter together: a generation method needs to produce useful data, handle substantial workloads, and accommodate requirements beyond the statistical summaries alone. PrivPGD is presented as addressing all three within private data synthesis.
icml-2024-privacy-preserving-data-releas.tldr: PrivPGD uses optimal transport and particle gradient descent for scalable private tabular-data synthesis with support for domain-specific constraints.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces a language model’s size by removing some of its weights. Post-training methods can do this without retraining, but their decisions depend on pruning metrics that often require expert design and repeated experimentation. Pruner-Zero automates the search for those metrics, targeting the rule used to decide which weights to remove.

The framework uses genetic programming to search over symbolic formulas. Its search space includes existing pruning metrics, allowing the procedure to explore alternatives within a broader family of expressions. An opposing-operation simplification strategy is introduced to increase population diversity during the search. The result is an automatically generated, explicit mathematical pruning metric.

Experiments on LLaMA and LLaMA-2 cover language modeling and zero-shot tasks. The authors report better performance than state-of-the-art post-training pruning methods in these evaluations. They also examine relationships between the discovered metrics and post-pruning performance, extracting principles from the search results. The approach thus serves both as a way to find effective pruning rules and as a tool for studying what makes such rules useful.
icml-2024-pruner-zero-evolving-symbolic-.tldr: Pruner-Zero automatically searches for symbolic pruning metrics and improves post-training pruning performance on the evaluated LLaMA models and tasks.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning becomes harder when labeled examples are unevenly distributed across classes and unlabeled examples have an unknown, potentially different class distribution. Assuming a fixed relationship between those distributions can restrict where a method works. SimPro addresses this setting without requiring predefined assumptions about the unlabeled class distribution.

The framework builds on a probabilistic model and modifies expectation-maximization by separating conditional distributions from marginal class distributions. This separation permits a closed-form class-distribution estimate during the maximization step. The resulting Bayes classifier then improves the pseudo-labels used in the expectation step, connecting distribution estimation with the assignment of provisional labels to unlabeled examples.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees and describe the framework as straightforward to implement. They also introduce two additional class distributions for evaluation, expanding the range of conditions tested. Across diverse benchmarks and distribution scenarios, SimPro achieves consistently state-of-the-art results. The significance is its adaptability when the available labeled data do not reliably indicate how common each class is in the unlabeled pool.
icml-2024-simpro-a-simple-probabilistic-.tldr: SimPro jointly refines class-distribution estimates and pseudo-labels to handle imbalanced labeled data and unknown, potentially mismatched unlabeled class distributions.

paragraphs: Optimization speed depends partly on the objective’s curvature, represented by the Hessian and its eigenvalues. Broad assumptions such as smoothness can hide distinctions between non-convex problems that matter for convergence. This paper introduces graded non-convexity to organize such problems into nested subclasses and make those distinctions more explicit.

The subclasses include familiar objectives arising in partially convex problems, matrix factorization, and neural networks. Building on this classification, the authors propose gradient methods with spectral preconditioning. These methods use approximate leading eigenvectors of the Hessian to address ill-conditioning in a way that depends on the problem’s grade.

For the applicable problem classes, the analysis proves better convergence rates than basic gradient descent. The improvements are especially relevant when there are large gaps between the leading Hessian eigenvalues. Numerical experiments on multiple practical machine-learning problems support the theory. The contribution connects a finer description of non-convex structure to an optimization method that can exploit that structure, giving more specific guidance than a single broad smoothness assumption.
icml-2024-spectral-preconditioning-for-g.tldr: Graded non-convexity identifies problem classes where Hessian-based spectral preconditioning provably improves convergence over basic gradient descent.

paragraphs: Predicting neural activity often means predicting when individual spikes occur. A common Poisson training objective instead represents activity as spike counts within fixed time intervals, typically 10 to 100 milliseconds. This can be a poor fit when neuronal responses carry timing precision down to a few milliseconds, where those models struggle.

The paper introduces a spike distance function: at every time point, its value is the temporal distance to the nearest spike. Neural networks are trained to approximate this function, making proximity to spike events the learning target. An efficient inference algorithm then converts the network’s predicted distance function into a spike train.

The authors evaluate the approach using recordings from chicken and frog retinal ganglion cells responding to visual stimuli. They compare it with Poisson models trained using different counting intervals and report better spike-train inference. The finding supports changing the target representation when precise event timing matters: learning distances to events provides a useful alternative to learning counts aggregated over intervals.
icml-2024-spike-distance-function-as-a-l.tldr: Learning the temporal distance to the nearest neural spike improves spike-train inference over Poisson models on the evaluated retinal recordings.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate high-quality samples, but their many sampling steps make generation slow. Consistency models address this by combining multiple steps into fewer operations. This paper develops statistical theory to explain how that faster sampling approach relates to the quality of the probability distribution learned during training.

The authors formulate consistency-model training as minimizing a discrepancy between distributions. They analyze estimation quality using Wasserstein distance, which provides a way to measure how far a learned distribution is from its target. This connects the training objective to a statistical account of how well the model estimates the desired distribution.

The resulting estimation rates match those established for ordinary diffusion models. The analysis covers consistency models trained through both distillation and isolation methods, extending its relevance across the two training routes. Matching rates provides theoretical support for the idea that accelerated sampling can coexist with strong distribution-estimation behavior. The contribution is a statistical explanation of consistency models’ advantage, complementing their motivation as a way to reduce generation steps.
icml-2024-theory-of-consistency-diffusio.tldr: The paper derives Wasserstein estimation rates for consistency models that match ordinary diffusion models across distillation and isolation training.

paragraphs: Time-series pre-training aims to learn useful representations before task-specific training, potentially reducing labeling needs. Methods adapted from language or vision can distort or overlook temporal relationships when they randomly mask observations or compare entire series. TimeSiam makes the relationship between earlier and later segments central to its learning task.

The framework uses Siamese encoders on randomly sampled past and current subseries. With simple augmentation such as masking, it learns through past-to-current reconstruction, encouraging representations that capture time-dependent structure across diverse segment pairs. Learnable lineage embeddings distinguish the temporal distances between sampled segments, helping the model represent different kinds of temporal correlation.

The authors evaluate forecasting and classification across 13 standard benchmarks, including settings within a domain and across domains. TimeSiam consistently outperforms the advanced pre-training baselines in these evaluations. The findings support using temporal relationships as an explicit organizing principle for pre-training: the placement of segments in time becomes part of what the model learns, alongside the contents of the segments themselves.
icml-2024-timesiam-a-pre-training-framew.tldr: TimeSiam learns relationships between past and current time-series segments, improving forecasting and classification across 13 evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Many learning objectives evaluate examples in pairs or larger groups instead of assigning a separate loss to each individual example. Understanding generalization in these settings is difficult because the losses are not independent and identically distributed, and the quantities being analyzed can become very high-dimensional. This paper develops a unified information-theoretic treatment of that problem.

The framework covers individual examples, pairs, triplets, quadruplets, and higher-order groupings. It provides two kinds of bounds. Hypothesis-based bounds analyze iterative, noisy learning algorithms through gradient covariance. Prediction-based bounds use low-dimensional information measures to estimate the generalization gap in a computationally tractable way.

These two perspectives connect generalization to both the learning process and the predictions it produces. Numerical studies across diverse learning settings show that the bounds capture generalization dynamics effectively. The contribution broadens the reach of information-theoretic analysis to objectives built from relationships among examples, giving a common framework for settings that are difficult to address through pointwise analysis alone.
icml-2024-towards-generalization-beyond-.tldr: A unified information-theoretic framework bounds generalization for learning objectives involving individual examples, pairs, and larger groups.

paragraphs: Detecting inputs that differ from training data is often approached in two ways: learning from labeled in-distribution examples or treating all such examples as one class. This paper asks when the class labels actually help distinguish familiar data from out-of-distribution data. The question concerns the value of label information for detection, beyond its use in ordinary classification.

The authors develop a graph-theoretic analysis of how well in-distribution and out-of-distribution data can be separated. They characterize representations through the graph’s spectral decomposition, enabling a closed-form analysis. From these representations, they establish a provable error bound comparing detection with and without in-distribution labels.

The bound reveals conditions under which labels improve detection, making their benefit conditional on the structure captured by the analysis. Experiments on simulated and real datasets validate the theoretical guarantees and support the resulting insights. The contribution provides a formal basis for understanding when supervised class information is useful for recognizing unfamiliar inputs, rather than assuming that labels always provide the same advantage.
icml-2024-when-and-how-does-in-distribut.tldr: A graph-based error analysis identifies conditions under which in-distribution class labels improve out-of-distribution detection.

paragraphs: Language-model agents can interact with software through a browser, but useful workplace automation requires evaluating them on tasks representative of daily knowledge work. WorkArena provides a remotely hosted benchmark with 33 tasks built around ServiceNow. Its focus is enterprise software use, placing agent evaluation in a setting tied to common professional workflows.

The paper also introduces BrowserGym, an environment for developing and evaluating browser agents. It supports a rich collection of actions and multimodal observations, providing the means for agents to perceive and operate the interface. Together, the benchmark and environment supply both the tasks to attempt and an infrastructure for studying how agents perform them.

The empirical evaluation finds promising capabilities alongside a substantial gap to full task automation. It also reveals a significant performance difference between open-source and closed-source language models. These findings make WorkArena useful for measuring progress while identifying unresolved capability gaps. The contribution is an evaluation setting that connects browser-agent research to the practical demands of enterprise knowledge work.
icml-2024-workarena-how-capable-are-web-.tldr: WorkArena and BrowserGym evaluate enterprise browser agents, revealing promising capabilities but a substantial remaining gap to full task automation.
